title: ICE almost deported this Eritrean woman to a third country after Canada turned her away
summary: Rahel Negassi is one of several asylum seekers who Canadian immigration lawyers say were erroneously denied entry into Canada and wound up in the murky, at times frightening world of ICE detention…

image.caption: Rahel Negassi spent two months in an ICE detention facility in Texas last year and was nearly deported to a third country after Canadian border agents denied her entry into Canada. She fought for a second chance and now lives in Kitchener, Ont., with her son. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Rahel Negassi was two months into her detention at a Texas Immigration Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in September 2025. Earlier that summer, the Eritrean woman had tried to claim asylum at the Canadian border where she was turned away, and she was about to be deported to a third country.

Negassi fled Eritrea's authoritarian government in the late '90s as it was entering one of many wars with neighbouring Ethiopia, taking a winding path from Sudan to the U.K., before landing in the U.S. in 2003. She spent nearly a year in immigration detention before her asylum application was rejected when her siblings weren't available to vouch for her. She was released as a paroled undocumented migrant, which meant regular check-ins with ICE.

She moved to Michigan, studied nursing and had two children, a daughter, now 18, and a son, now 13. She lived in the U.S. for two decades without issue, under authorizations the U.S. government provided her to work as a nurse because they could not deport her to Eritrea.

But after Trump was re-elected, ICE began deportation proceedings and Negassi spent months preparing to move to Canada with her son. She gathered the necessary documents, including the results of a DNA test proving her connection to her brother in Canada. That qualified her for one of the few exceptions to Canada's Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA) with the U.S.
Negassi's case seemed, to her, so certain. She never thought they'd be turned away.

items: What is the Safe Third Country agreement?

blocks.text: "I was not scared. I thought: 'I already have the DNA test. More than DNA, what can you bring?'" Negassi told CBC in a recent interview from Kitchener, Ont., where she and her son now live.

Negassi, 51, is one of several asylum seekers who were erroneously denied entry into Canada, then wound up in the murky, at times frightening, world of ICE detention since U.S. President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, according to Canadian lawyers who have taken on their cases.
Canadian border agents skeptical
When she arrived at the Canadian border on June 27, 2025, Negassi says border agents immediately expressed skepticism that she was really born in Eritrea.
"He said, 'Just tell me you are Ethiopian. I know you guys pretend to be Eritrean and you come to Canada and you ask asylum,'" Negassi said.

Then, at her official interview, she says the officer expressed doubt and called her brother to verify facts, but they had been separated for decades. When the agent returned, Negassi was informed she was being found ineligible to enter Canada. Even the DNA tests, approved by a company endorsed by the Canada Border Services Agency, weren't enough.

items: 2 families rejected at Canadian border are now mired in what lawyer calls a 'black hole' of ICE detention

blocks.text: She spent four or five days in a detention facility at the U.S. border with her son before they were separated — he went to live with his stepfather, a U.S. citizen. Negassi was ushered onto a flight bound for an ICE detention centre in El Valle, Texas.
Her husband contacted Ottawa-based immigration lawyer Heather Neufeld as soon as he found out the two had been detained.
Heather Neufeld, an Ottawa immigration lawyer, represented Negassi and helped push for her case to be reconsidered at the Canadian border last year. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Lawyers challenge border agreement

Neufeld has overseen many cases similar to Negassi's. She's part of a team of lawyers representing a constitutional challenge to the STCA, which bars most asylum seekers from entering Canada through the U.S.

According to statistics the team cited in Federal Court earlier this month, at least 4,323 people were found ineligible to enter Canada and were returned to the U.S. between Jan. 1, 2025 and March 30, 2026. One-fifth of them were children.

items: Federal Court challenge says Canada failing to protect refugees turned back to U.S.

blocks.text: "The percentage of people who would manage to access counsel on these turn-back cases is minuscule," Neufeld told CBC News. "All the rest of these people … are just summarily deported."

On behalf of Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees and the Canadian Council of Churches, the lawyers argue the STCA violates equality rights under section 15 of the Canadian Charter because it disproportionately harms vulnerable groups, such as racialized people, women, children and 2SLGBTQ+ individuals.
They say those groups, namely women fleeing gender violence and 2SLGBTQ+ people, are overlooked by U.S. asylum law and face harrowing conditions and family separations in immigration detention.
How ICE detention is forcing immigrants out of the U.S.

Though that was also the case under previous U.S. administrations, Julia Sande, a lawyer specializing in privacy and migrant rights at Amnesty International Canada says "things are so much worse right now," making the constitutional challenge even more urgent.

What's more, Canadian border agents do not appear to be informing asylum claimants that they may qualify to come to Canada if they can prove they face personal dangers, such as death, extreme sanction, inhumane treatment or a real risk of forced deportation, without evaluation in the U.S. These "safety valves" are listed in a 2023 Supreme Court decision on the STCA's constitutionality.
Sande says this process is opaque and not publicly available. "It's not clear to anyone, let alone an unrepresented refugee showing up at the border, what on Earth you would need to do," she said.

items: How ICE detention is forcing immigrants out of the U.S.

blocks.text: Lawyers representing the federal government have argued that the claims presented in the constitutional challenge are moot, because most of the asylum claimants cited now have status in Canada.

In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada said the border agreement "is designed to keep the Canada–U.S. border safe and well-managed. It helps avoid sudden spikes in asylum claims that could overwhelm border crossings, housing, and processing systems."
Negassi says it took her months to recover from her time at an ICE detention centre in Texas last year. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
One of the lucky ones
Negassi says she was one of the lucky ones.

After Neufeld filed a request for judicial review of Negassi's case in the summer of 2025, the Canadian Department of Justice arranged for ICE to have her sent back to the Canadian border on Sept. 2, 2025.
Negassi says her earlier optimism was replaced by the cold fear of being turned away by Canada again. However, this time, when she was accompanied by Neufeld, she was let in.
"When they say the United States is safe … the United States is not safe for anybody at this time," she said.
"It was bad. It was so bad," Negassi said of her border experience and being detained by ICE, which she says transported her back in time to her journey to flee Eritrea.

items: Shackled, abused and humiliated: Report paints grim picture of life in ICE detention

blocks.text: "You are in fight or flight. You do everything — your energy, everything — just to survive," Negassi said, recalling both her experience as a young asylum seeker and, then again last year.

She's been working to obtain her Canadian nursing licence and says she's only now recovering from the ordeal. Still, she says she's grateful to have made it to Canada with her son and once again feels safe and is rebuilding her life.
"I want to show Canadians, everybody — you see, I made it," she said. "I'm still OK. The United States didn't break me."
Negassi, who is Pentecostal Christian, has been advocating for human rights causes in her home country of Eritrea from abroad. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
